Photograph: Julie Sebadelha/AFP/Getty Images Opinion France The Guardian view on the French left: division makes Marine Le Pen’s path to the Élysée more straightforward Editorial Two years ago, progressive parties allied to see off the far right in a parliamentary election. Ahead of a seismic presidential election, that unity is missing Tue 25 Aug 2026 13.27 EDT Last modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 13.55 EDT Share I n the summer of 2024, as polls suggested that Marine Le Pen’s far-right Rassemblement National party would win a snap legislative election rashly called by Emmanuel Macron, the perennially fragmented French left united to spectacular effect. The New Popular Front, whose name evoked Léon Blum’s anti-fascist alliance in the 1930s, came first in a poll that delivered a hung parliament. Eight months before a presidential contest in which Ms Le Pen is the clear frontrunner, the prospect of a repeat performance appears close to zero. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the hard-left France Unbowed, and Olivier Faure, the leader of the Socialist party (PS), have both ruled out the idea of backing a single candidate. Efforts by the Greens to broker talks between progressive parties have fallen on deaf ears. The obvious danger, as the most important election in the history of the Fifth Republic looms, is that chronic division will ease Ms Le Pen’s path to the Élysée. The 75-year-old Mr Mélenchon is a deeply polarising figure who has failed three times to reach the second round of a presidential race. But in a fractured field, the loyalty of his base among the young, the urban precariat and ethnic minority voters gives him a credible chance of making the runoff this time. At which point, polls predict , France’s traditional “Republican front” against the far right would disintegrate, handing Ms Le Pen a crushing victory. Within the PS, the picture is one of confusion and debilitating internal rivalries. Raphael Glucksmann, the leader of Public Square, a small sister movement, declared his candidacy on Sunday and is favourite to win a joint primary. But senior figures such as the former president François Hollande are rumoured to be waiting to make their own move later on. The Greens are divided over whether to offer support to Mr Mélenchon’s uncompromising leftism and reward his new emphasis on the environment, or back Mr Glucksmann’s more centrist strategy. View image in fullscreen Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Photograph: Raphaël Lafargue/Abaca/Shutterstock All of which makes Mr Glucksmann’s stated ambition to “rebuild the left” seem somewhat optimistic. A Parisian intellectual married to a famous television newsreader (who has taken leave for the duration of the campaign), he is polling at 10% and is unburdened by the aura of failure that has dogged the Socialist party in recent years. But if he becomes its presidential candidate, he will face the same challenge as his immediate predecessors: how to reconnect with alienated blue-collar towns that now vote for Ms Le Pen, while simultaneously courting Mr Mélenchon’s urban radicals and reassuring middle-class voters who deserted for Mr Macron. In 2022, the former Paris mayor Anne Hidalgo comprehensively flunked that test, receiving 1.75% of votes cast. A historic humiliation was partly the result of progressive voters calculating that Mr Mélenchon was the left candidate with the best chance of coming second, thus excluding Ms Le Pen from the runoff. But as the 2027 campaign begins in earnest, she enjoys a 20-point lead in the polls, and another place in the second round is all but assured. The question, therefore, is who can rally enough support from across the political spectrum to stop her becoming president. A united left would have had a far better chance of coming up with a convincing answer. But that is not the left France currently has. Then ICE Offers Him a Way Out To Avoid Criminal Charges Drunk Pilot Steals a Plane and Flies Dangerously Close to a Nuclear Plant at 20,000 Feet Before Crashing Into a Sunflower Field By Umme Tun Nessa Sep 1st, 2026, 9:47 am Save us as a preferred source in Google Share Share Share Flying too close to a nuclear power plant is enough to get the military’s attention. But when the aircraft was allegedly stolen and the person flying it was reportedly intoxicated, the situation became much more serious. Small aircraft can end up at the center of some dangerous situations, including a recent case where a Cessna 172 tore through a woman’s paraglider . This time, another Cessna 172 caused concern after entering restricted airspace near a nuclear power plant in Hungary. According to the New York Post , a 24-year-old man allegedly took the aircraft from a nearby airport without permission. Fighter jets were sent after the plane, but the incident ended in a sunflower field just miles from Hungary’s only nuclear power plant. So much for a quiet morning in Hungary The incident happened on the morning of Aug. 29, when authorities say the man took a Cessna 172 from Kalocsa Airport without authorization. Hungarian military radar detected the aircraft as it flew toward the Paks Nuclear Power Plant, prompting the country’s air force to send two Gripen fighter jets to the area. The airspace around Paks receives special protection because of the nuclear facility. Civilian aircraft are prohibited from flying within roughly two miles of the plant at altitudes below 20,000 feet. The facility reportedly generates about half of Hungary’s electricity and was not damaged during the incident. A pilot was detained in Hungary after allegedly stealing a plane while intoxicated, triggering a fighter jet scramble before making an emergency landing in a sunflower field and trying to flee. pic.twitter.com/el4s8FONMP — Breaking911 (@Breaking911) August 30, 2026 Only minutes after the fighter jets were dispatched, the Cessna made a forced landing in a sunflower field near Gerjen. The Gripens located the damaged plane and remained above the area until a rescue helicopter and emergency crews arrived. Authorities reported no injuries from the landing. An aircraft making it safely back to the ground after an unexpected danger in its flight path would normally bring the immediate concern to an end. For the man in Hungary, however, landing the Cessna was apparently not the end of the trouble. Police say the man left the aircraft behind and was later spotted walking along Route 512 in a confused state. A passing driver stopped to help him, but the 24-year-old allegedly got into the vehicle and attempted to drive away before the motorist stopped him. Officers arrived within minutes and arrested the man. According to Hungarian police, information available to investigators indicated that he was intoxicated, while authorities were still examining whether he had been under the influence of any other substances. Police opened proceedings over the unauthorized taking of a vehicle and other alleged offenses. Authorities are now investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident, including how the Cessna was taken from Kalocsa Airport. Hungarian police also announced a joint inspection of that airport with aviation authorities, with checks expected to follow at other airports across the country. Have a tip we should know?
